Repair or replace: compare future cash, current resale value and a common exit date

Use cash-flow bridges, cumulative costs and a signed sensitivity matrix to separate an old purchase price from the money that changes in today’s repair decision.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare the cash that changes from today at one common exit date

Interactive planning lab

Present value of future net cost: repair and retain$1,874.58
Present value of future net cost: replace now$2,122.56
Replacement minus repair present cost; negative favours replacement$247.97

Original deterministic nominal-CAD illustration. The entered original purchase price of CAD 2,200 is already paid and unrecoverable; it is context only and never enters the forward costs. Each option is assumed to provide the same required service throughout the common whole-year horizon, without another failure, replacement or difference in usage. Repair is paid at time zero. Replacement purchase and installation are paid at time zero, less net proceeds from selling the old item at that same time. Running costs are constant nominal amounts paid at each year-end. Each item is sold for its independently entered net value at the common final year-end, after that year’s running cost. No intermediate sale is assumed. Present values use the entered effective annual nominal discount rate; they are alternatives to undiscounted totals, not additional bills. No loan, interest charge, tax calculation, refund, warranty recovery, inflation forecast, service interruption or environmental benefit is modeled. Costs may be negative if entered sale receipts exceed outlays. Changing the past-price context does not change any metric or chart.

The central idea

Begin the comparison today. Include a repair quote, replacement costs, sale proceeds and future running costs once, using the same service requirement and exit date.

01

Write the two forward alternatives before looking at the original receipt

An expensive item can feel worth repairing because it cost a lot when new. A disappointing past purchase can also make replacement feel like an admission of loss. The forward cash question is more concrete: what money changes from today if the household repairs and retains the item, compared with replacing it now?

The illustration assumes that either alternative provides the same required service for five more years. The old item can be repaired for CAD 450. A replacement costs CAD 1,600, with CAD 150 of delivery and installation. Its assumed annual running cost is lower. Both alternatives are evaluated at the same final date, including independently entered net sale values.

The original CAD 2,200 purchase payment is already paid and unrecoverable. The context field lets you change that past amount, but doing so intentionally leaves every cost metric and chart unchanged. The numbers that can change the forward choice have their own inputs.

02

Distinguish an unrecoverable past payment from sale proceeds available today

ACCA’s relevant-cost guidance distinguishes past costs from changes in future cash and explains the opportunity cost of keeping an asset that could otherwise be sold. That distinction is the accounting context for this original household example; the source does not provide the repair quotes, resale estimates or discount rate used here.

The old item’s assumed net sale value today is CAD 100. Replacing it allows that receipt now, so the replacement cash calculation is CAD 1,600 + CAD 150 − CAD 100 = CAD 1,650. Repairing it uses CAD 450 and keeps the item. The initial replacement outlay is therefore CAD 1,200 higher.

The CAD 100 is relevant because the two choices change whether it is received today. It is different from the historical CAD 2,200 payment. No fraction of the original receipt is added to today’s repair payment merely because that receipt once existed.

03

Count the current resale opportunity once

The same initial difference can be expressed using two consistent ledgers. The cash ledger compares CAD 450 to repair with CAD 1,650 to replace after selling the old item. An equivalent opportunity-cost ledger adds the common CAD 100 resale baseline to both sides: CAD 550 for retaining and repairing the old item, versus CAD 1,750 for acquiring and installing the replacement before sale proceeds.

Both comparisons give the same CAD 1,200 difference. The opportunity-cost presentation makes the sale receipt forgone by retaining the item visible; it does not create another CAD 100 invoice.

Combining the two ledgers incorrectly would add the CAD 100 forgone sale to repair and subtract it from replacement. That would count the same opportunity twice and produce a false CAD 1,100 difference. The calculator uses the cash ledger throughout: the old sale appears once as a receipt in the replacement alternative.

04

Follow running costs and the final sale through the same five years

After repair, the old item has an assumed constant running cost of CAD 320 per year. The replacement costs CAD 180 per year to run. These are all-in scenario inputs, not measured electricity consumption, market tariffs or quoted maintenance plans. They can include the recurring costs relevant to the comparison if the same categories are used on both sides.

The old item’s assumed final net sale value is zero, so its five-year undiscounted net cost is CAD 450 + 5 × CAD 320 = CAD 2,050. The replacement has an assumed CAD 400 final sale receipt, giving CAD 1,650 + 5 × CAD 180 − CAD 400 = CAD 2,150.

The replacement line falls from CAD 2,370 at year four to CAD 2,150 at year five because the final CAD 400 receipt exceeds that last year’s CAD 180 running cost. The decline does not mean a negative operating bill. A sale receipt is included only at the selected final date, after the last running-cost payment.

05

Compare present values without adding them to the cash bills

The default effective annual nominal discount rate is an assumed 4%. Initial payments remain at today’s value. Annual running payments are discounted from each year-end, and final sale receipts from the common exit date. Under those assumptions, repair has a present net cost of about CAD 1,874.58 and replacement about CAD 2,122.56.

The replacement-minus-repair bridge begins with CAD 1,200 of additional initial cash. The present value of its CAD 140 annual running-cost reduction subtracts about CAD 623.26. Its additional CAD 400 exit receipt subtracts about CAD 328.77 after discounting. The remaining difference is about CAD 247.97 of higher present cost for replacement.

That differs from the CAD 100 undiscounted difference because the replacement’s offsetting savings and sale receipt occur later than its additional initial payment. Present value is an alternative valuation of the same cash schedule. It is not another charge, an interest bill, a promised investment return or permission to ignore the cash needed now.

06

Stress the uncertain quote and running cost before interpreting the answer

The matrix replaces the repair quote and the replacement’s annual running cost. It holds the selected horizon, old running cost, discount rate, current sale receipt and both final sale values fixed. Each cell is replacement present cost minus repair present cost: a positive amount means replacement costs more in the model; a negative amount means it costs less.

A lower running-cost estimate cannot by itself establish that a replacement is preferable. The price difference, timing and exit values still enter the same comparison. Likewise, a higher repair quote can change the result without changing the amount originally paid for the old item.

The five-year service assumption is a condition of the illustration, not a reliability finding. A repair that provides less service, another breakdown, a different replacement cycle or a change in usage needs additional dated cash flows. Changing the horizon also requires reviewing both final sale values rather than treating them as guaranteed amounts at any date.

07

Make the forward comparison usable in a household budget

  1. Confirm the required service and a common comparison date.
  2. Obtain current repair, purchase, delivery and installation amounts.
  3. Use net sale receipts after selling costs, with realistic receipt dates.
  4. Compare running costs on the same usage and dollar basis.
  5. Review final values, remaining service life and the cash available today.

The calculator assumes cash settlement today and no financing, tax calculation, refund, warranty recovery, inflation or another failure. It does not value convenience, downtime or differences in product quality. If the old item’s sale receipt arrives after the new purchase payment, the upfront bridge understates the interim cash needed and a separate timing plan is required.

A forward cost comparison helps identify the amounts that matter. The household still needs a workable payment plan and evidence that each option can provide the service being compared.
